newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy sets shareholder rules for telecom firm Stet.
newsitem.headline: Italy sets shareholder rules for telecom firm Stet.

text.p: The Italian Treasury on Monday laid out shareholdership rules for telecoms group Stet following its planned sell-off later this year, fixing three percent as the maximum stake any one investor can take in the company.

The Treasury added that it expected to keep a so-called 'golden share' in Stet for up to three years following the privatisation, allowing it to maintain special rights over the firm once it loses majority control.
The Stet sale, dubbed the mother of all privatisations, is due to take place this October after the holding is merged with its fixed-line telephone unit Telecom Italia.

However legislation needed for the sell-off, including a bill to create a watchdog body, has still not been approved by parliament and commentators say that if the regulatory body is not ratified by May, the sell-off might be postponed again.

The Treasury said on Monday the golden share would be dropped once the watchdog body had consolidated its position and when the liberalisation of the domestic telecoms market had reached "a sufficiently advanced level."
"This might take less than three years, but it could take more," a spokeswoman at the Treasury said.

The golden share will include clauses giving the state the right to veto the entry of new major shareholders, the right to veto any planned break-up of the group and the right to a certain number of board members.
Italy has employed a similar mechanism for the privatisation of energy group ENI.
The Treasury currently holds just over 61 percent of Stet's ordinary capital and has already said it wants to create a stable core of shareholders in the company when control passes to private hands.
"The Treasury fixes three percent as the reference point for the exercising of special rights," Monday's statement said, adding that three percent would also be the maximum holding permitted.
The new shareholder rules approved by the Treasury on Monday still have to be rubber-stamped by parliament.
